title: The Psychology of Being Broke: 20 Mental Traps
description:
Being broke is usually not a knowledge problem. It's a psychology problem. In this video I go through 20 mental traps that keep smart, hardworking people broke, from three angles: the ways our brains get money math wrong, the emotional traps of fear, comparison and avoidance, and the research-backed playbook that actually helps people get unstuck.

Get The Ryan Rover Money Playbook: [LINK HERE]

0:00 Intro
1:56 How we got the research
2:38 Angle 1: The Numbers
2:44 1. Anchoring
3:57 2. Mental accounting
5:04 3. Present bias
6:08 4. Exponential growth bias
7:25 5. The sunk cost trap
8:26 6. The pain of paying
9:28 7. The power of free
10:27 Why smart people fall for these
11:41 Angle 2: The Psychology
11:59 8. The scarcity tunnel
12:54 9. The ostrich effect
13:55 10. Social comparison
14:47 11. Hedonic adaptation
16:05 12. Status quo bias
17:02 13. Optimism bias
17:56 14. Loss aversion
18:52 The emotions behind money
20:22 Angle 3: The Playbook
20:38 15. Decision fatigue
21:39 16. No commitment device
22:45 17. A broke identity
23:39 18. Learned helplessness
24:32 19. Planning fallacy
25:26 20. Going it alone
26:15 A day full of traps
27:57 How businesses use these traps
29:28 Your anti trap toolkit
30:38 Questions people ask
32:56 Recap: all 20 traps
33:34 What to do next

Sources:
- Mani, Mullainathan, Shafir and Zhao, Poverty Impedes Cognitive Function (Science, 2013); Mullainathan and Shafir, Scarcity (2013)
- Tversky and Kahneman, Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases (Science, 1974); Kahneman and Tversky, Prospect Theory (1979); Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011)
- Richard Thaler, mental accounting; Thaler and Benartzi, Save More Tomorrow (Journal of Political Economy, 2004)
- Stango and Zinman, Exponential Growth Bias and Household Finance (Journal of Finance, 2009)
- Arkes and Blumer, The Psychology of Sunk Cost (1985); Prelec and Simester, Always Leave Home Without It (Marketing Letters, 2001)
- Shampanier, Mazar and Ariely, Zero as a Special Price (Marketing Science, 2007)
- Karlsson, Loewenstein and Seppi, The Ostrich Effect (2009); Agarwal, Mikhed and Scholnick, Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia (lottery neighbors)
- Brickman, Coates and Janoff-Bulman, Lottery Winners and Accident Victims (1978); Tali Sharot, The Optimism Bias (2011)
- Madrian and Shea, The Power of Suggestion (Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2001); Iyengar and Lepper, When Choice is Demotivating (2000)
- Martin Seligman, learned helplessness; American Psychological Association, Stress in America
- Growth example: monthly compounding at 7% average yearly return (illustration, not a promise)
